title: Diameter of Binary Tree
directAnswer: The diameter is the longest path (counted in edges) between any two nodes — it need not pass through the root. Run one post-order DFS where each node returns its height (1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)). At every node, the longest path bending there is leftHeight + rightHeight edges; update a global maximum with that. Return the height upward, record the split globally. O(n) time, O(h) space.

remember.pattern: Post-order DFS returning height while a global max records left + right
remember.formula:
self.best = 0
def height(node):
    if not node: return 0
    L = height(node.left)
    R = height(node.right)
    self.best = max(self.best, L + R)   # path bending here, in EDGES
    return 1 + max(L, R)                # height returned to parent
rules: Diameter is measured in **edges**, not nodes — a single node has diameter 0, two nodes have diameter 1.
A node **returns** `1 + max(L, R)` (one branch, its height) — the parent extends a single chain.
A node **updates the global** with `L + R` (both branches) — the longest path that bends at this node.
Use **post-order**: you cannot compute `L` and `R` until both children have reported their heights.
Define empty subtree height as **0** so a leaf returns height 1 and its bending path is `0 + 0 = 0` edges.
whenToUse: Longest path / distance between two nodes in a tree where the path can bend at one node
When the value you return to a parent differs from the value you record globally
Any tree metric that combines two child results at a node but extends only one upward
Width / depth style questions where each node contributes a 'through me' candidate
antiSignals: Path must be root-to-leaf only → simple top-down depth, no global split needed
You need the actual node sequence, not the length → reconstruct, more bookkeeping
Graph with cycles, not a tree → BFS two-pass (farthest node twice) instead of DFS
Weighted edges → carry edge weights instead of counting 1 per edge
remember.takeaway: Diameter is the textbook case of 'return partial, record full': the height handed upward uses one child so a parent can keep a straight chain, while the global captures the bend through both children. The same engine solves Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Longest Univalue Path.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you separate two values in one DFS — the height you return upward versus the bending path (left + right) you record globally — and whether you count edges, not nodes.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning `1 + L + R` upward (mixing height with the bending path), or counting nodes so every answer is off by one, or recomputing height per node and shipping an O(n²) solution.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the brute force (height-per-node, O(n²)) first, then collapse it into one post-order pass. Name the 'return height, record split' pattern and tie it to Maximum Path Sum.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the length of the diameter*** of the tree.

The ***diameter*** of a binary tree is the length of the ***longest path*** between any two nodes in the tree. This path may or may not pass through the `root`.

The length of a path between two nodes is represented by the ***number of edges*** between them.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
The path length is counted in edges, so a single-node tree has diameter 0
understanding: We want the longest chain of edges connecting two nodes anywhere in the tree. The chain peaks (bends) at exactly one node — its highest point — where it may dip into both subtrees. Node values are irrelevant; only the shape matters. The answer is a count of edges, so be careful not to count nodes by mistake.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the diameter measured in nodes or edges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Edges. A single node is diameter 0; a root with two children is diameter 2. Counting nodes gives an off-by-one answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the longest path have to pass through the root?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. It can peak at any node, which is exactly why we track a global maximum across every node rather than just checking the root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say at least one node, but a clean solution returns 0 for an empty tree anyway — the empty-subtree height of 0 handles it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the tree be deeply skewed (a near-linked-list)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, up to 10⁴ deep. Recursion is fine here, but mention that an explicit stack avoids a stack overflow if the depth limit were larger.

examples.explanation: The path 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 (or 5 → 2 → 1 → 3) has 3 edges and bends at the root.
Two nodes, one edge between them.
A single node has no edges, so the diameter is 0 — this is why the answer counts edges.

diagrams.title: Height up, split recorded
diagrams.caption: Return 1 + max(L, R) to the parent; record L + R (the bending path in edges) as a global candidate.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Height Computed at Every Node
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to frame the problem ('every path bends at some node') before collapsing it into one pass.
hints: Every path has a single highest node where it bends. Fix that node: what is the longest path that bends exactly there?
The longest path bending at node X is height(X.left) + height(X.right) edges. Take the maximum of that over all nodes.
Computing height(X) is itself a recursion over a subtree. Calling it for every node independently repeats work — that is the O(n²).
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n nodes we compute the height of its two subtrees, each an O(n) DFS in the worst case → O(n²) time. Recursion depth is bounded by the tree height → O(h) space.
approaches.explanation:
Begin from the observation that *every* path peaks at exactly one node — the unique highest point where it can branch into both subtrees. So the diameter is the maximum, over all nodes, of 'longest path that bends at this node'.

**The path that bends at a node.** Let `height(x)` be the number of edges on the longest downward chain from `x` to any leaf, with an empty subtree having height 0. The longest path bending at node `p` uses the deepest chain on each side: `height(p.left) + height(p.right)` edges. The diameter is the maximum of this quantity across all nodes.

**Why it counts edges cleanly.** Each `height` is an edge count, and joining a left chain and a right chain at `p` simply adds the two edge counts — `p` itself contributes no extra edge because it is the meeting point. A leaf has `0 + 0 = 0`, which is correct.

**Why it is quadratic.** Computing `height(x)` walks the whole subtree under `x`. If we call it once per node as a separate pass, the same heights are recomputed again and again — n nodes × O(n) per height = O(n²). For n = 10⁴ that is up to ~10⁸ operations, slow and wasteful.

**Why mention it.** It nails the framing — 'paths bend at a node, combine two downward arms' — that the optimal reuses. The jump to O(n) is just: compute each height *once* and fold the bend check into the same traversal.
approaches.insight: Realizing every path has a single bend point turns a scary 'all pairs of nodes' search into 'for each node, the longest path that bends here'. The only inefficiency is recomputing heights; doing each height once in a post-order pass is the whole optimization.

dryRun.intro: Try each node as the bend point; the largest left-height + right-height wins.

java.explanation: Longest path bending at root: left chain edges plus right chain edges.
Also consider paths that bend somewhere inside the left subtree.
height(): recomputed per node → the O(n²) blow-up.

python.explanation: Edges on the longest downward chain; empty subtree is 0.
Both arms combined — the path that bends at this node, in edges.
Max over this bend and bends in either subtree; repeated height() calls cause O(n²).

pitfalls: Recomputing height() for every node — the source of the quadratic cost.
Counting nodes instead of edges — every answer comes out one too large.
Forgetting the bend uses BOTH arms while height() uses only one.

approaches.name: Single Post-Order DFS — Height Up, Split Recorded (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. 'One DFS: each node returns its height; I update a global max with left + right.'
hints: In the brute force, height(x) was recomputed everywhere. What if each node computed its height exactly once and handed it up?
Have the recursion return the height (one branch). At the same node, while you hold both children's heights, compute the bending path (left + right edges) and update a global best.
Return 1 + max(L, R) upward, but record L + R as the global diameter candidate. One traversal, no second pass.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single post-order visit touches each node once with O(1) work → O(n) time. The only extra memory is the recursion stack, bounded by the tree height → O(h) space.
approaches.explanation:
Fold the whole computation into one post-order DFS. The trick is to keep two related quantities strictly apart.

**Quantity 1 — the height returned upward.** When the recursion finishes a node, it returns the length of the longest downward chain from this node: `1 + max(L, R)`, where `L` and `R` are the children's heights. We return only one branch because the parent will attach this node as a link in a straight chain — a chain cannot pass through both children of a node and still continue upward.

**Quantity 2 — the global best (the bend).** At the *same* node we ask: what is the longest path whose highest point is this node? It dips into both children, giving `L + R` edges. This value is *not* returned upward (a path cannot both fork here and extend to the parent), but it is a candidate for the overall diameter, so we fold it into a global maximum.

**Why these must differ.** This is the whole difficulty. If you returned `L + R` (or `1 + L + R`) to the parent, the parent could attach a path that already used both of this node's branches and *still* extend upward — an impossible shape that revisits the node. Returning only the single best branch keeps every upward extension a legal straight chain, while the global captures the legal bends.

**Why post-order.** A node cannot compute either quantity until it knows both children's heights, so we must finish the children before the parent — that is post-order (left, right, then node).

**Edges versus nodes again.** Because `height` counts edges (empty subtree = 0, leaf = 1 returned but `0 + 0 = 0` recorded), `L + R` is automatically an edge count. If you instead made `height` count nodes, you would have to subtract along the way — easier to just count edges from the start.
approaches.insight: The pattern is 'return a partial result, record a complete result'. The upward return is deliberately weaker (one branch, the height) than the value scored globally (two branches, the bend) because they answer different questions: 'how deep am I for my parent to extend?' versus 'what is the longest path that peaks at me?'. This exact split powers Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Longest Univalue Path.

dryRun.intro: Post-order. Each node returns its height; global best records left + right (edges). best starts at 0.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: 'TreeNode') -> int:
    self.best = 0

    def height(node: 'TreeNode') -> int:
        if node is None:
            return 0
        left = height(node.left)
        right = height(node.right)
        self.best = max(self.best, left + right)   # bend here, in edges
        return 1 + max(left, right)                # height up to parent

    height(root)
    return self.best

java.explanation: Smallest possible diameter is 0 (single node), so 0 is a safe floor.
Child heights must be known first — that is why this is post-order.
Record the bending path peaking here (BOTH arms, edges) as a global candidate.
Return only ONE branch's height so the parent extends a legal straight chain.

python.explanation: Diameter is at least 0; no need for −∞ since lengths are non-negative.
Post-order: compute child heights before the parent does anything.
Both arms combined is the longest path that bends at this node — global only.
Hand the parent a single-branch height; never the sum.

edgeCases.behavior: Leaf: left=right=0, bend = 0 → best = 0; returns 1. Counting edges gives the correct 0.
No bend uses two arms; best ends up the full depth − 0 = number of edges down the chain (3).
Recursion depth equals the chain length; mention an explicit stack if depth could exceed the language limit.

pitfalls: Returning left + right (or 1 + left + right) upward — allows an illegal path that forks and still extends.
Counting nodes instead of edges — every result is one too large.
Recursing without a depth guard on pathological skewed trees — risk of stack overflow on very deep inputs.

commonMistakes: Counting nodes instead of edges, so every answer is off by one.
Returning the bend value (left + right) to the parent instead of the height (1 + max).
Recomputing height at every node and shipping an O(n²) solution.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting nodes instead of edges
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The diameter is defined in edges. If height counts nodes, a single node reports height 1 and a leaf-to-leaf path comes out one too large. Count edges from the start: empty subtree = 0, and the bend is left + right.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
left = height(node.left)
right = height(node.right)
self.best = max(self.best, left + right)   # edges, no off-by-one
return 1 + max(left, right)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the bend sum upward
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The value handed to the parent must be a straight downward chain (one child). Returning left + right lets the parent extend a path that already used both of this node's branches — a shape that would revisit the node.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
best = Math.max(best, left + right);
return left + right;        // illegal: both branches handed up
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
best = Math.max(best, left + right);
return 1 + Math.max(left, right);   // one branch up

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Two-pass height recomputation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Calling a separate height() inside a per-node loop recomputes the same subtree heights repeatedly, turning an O(n) problem into O(n²). Fold the height into the same DFS that records the global best.

followupVariations.title: Longest Univalue Path
followupVariations.hint: Return the longest same-value arm upward; record left arm + right arm (same value) globally.

followupVariations.hint: For a general tree given as edges, either the same DFS over an adjacency list, or BFS from the farthest node twice.

followupVariations.hint: The height subroutine on its own — the building block this problem extends.

patternNote: Post-order DFS that returns a partial (single-branch height) value while recording a complete (both-branch) value globally. Reach for it whenever a tree path can bend at a node but the value handed to a parent must stay a straight chain. Same engine as Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Longest Univalue Path.
